name: Ivan Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and isn't linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the organist at St Michael's, the parish church in our town, which is part-time and paid by the parish. Sunday mass, Thursday choir practice, and funerals and weddings when they come, which is most weeks. Saturdays in summer I play accordion with my uncle Josef's folk band at weddings and village festivals. I'm not a trained organist really, I learned from old Mr Brandt before he retired, and I still get the pedals wrong in the big hymns.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a good week look like, and a hard one?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A good week is two funerals, a wedding and a full church on Sunday, and I'm sorry to say funerals pay the bills. A hard week is when Father Tomasz tells me the collection was down again. I'm engaged to Marta, who's a teaching assistant at the primary school, and we're saving for the wedding. We've about three months of money put aside. I don't use any AI things, I'm not even sure what they'd do for an organist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people have more sense than the newspapers thought. I'd say it after mass, to the choir, over coffee. I'm not one for the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my worry isn't machines, it's empty pews. The congregation is mostly over seventy and every year there are fewer. That's where my wage comes from, the collection and the fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep playing, keep the weddings with Josef, and save for our own wedding. I'd maybe ask Father Tomasz if the parish next door needs an organist too, so I can cover two churches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but a bit sad. Not about AI. About the church getting quieter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long do you think the parish can keep paying an organist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe ten years, maybe less, if the collection keeps falling. I play for more funerals than weddings at St Michael's (his parish church), and one day there won't be enough people left to pay the organist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever think about leaving the church job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not by choice. It's where I was baptised. I'd find a second job before I'd leave the organ.

say: I'd say people have **more sense** than the newspapers thought.
I'd say it after mass over **coffee**, not online.
think: My real worry is **empty pews**, not machines.
My wage depends on a **shrinking congregation**, mostly over seventy.
do: Keep playing at **St Michael's** and at weddings with Josef's band.
Ask about covering a **second parish** as organist.
feel: **Steady** but a bit **sad** about the church getting quieter.
S0.quote: I play for more funerals than weddings at St Michael's (his parish church), and one day there won't be enough people left to pay the organist.
fieldNote: His pressure is a **falling collection**, which AI doesn't change.
He ties his work closely to **faith and place**, not just money.
He's never used AI and **doesn't see a use** for it.

steps.text: Keep playing Sunday mass, funerals and weddings at St Michael's
Ask the neighbouring parish if it needs an organist
Put aside money each month for the wedding with Marta

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a parish isn't a business, and nobody wants a machine playing at their mother's funeral. I'd say that to anyone. I'd also say people should look after each other instead of waiting for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, some churches already use a digital organ that plays hymns by itself. If the parish council is short of money, they'll look at it. Father Tomasz wouldn't want it, but he doesn't control the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself useful in other ways, run the children's choir, help with the parish hall. I'd keep the band weddings with Josef because people still want live music at a village wedding. I won't learn any computer things for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be watching the parish council meetings more closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the parish council would push for the digital organ?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hartmann, the treasurer. A good man, but he counts everything. Mr Hartmann (the parish treasurer) would buy a self-playing organ tomorrow if it saved the parish four hundred euros a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a funeral needs someone watching the family, slowing down when the widow can't sing. The machine doesn't see that. I'd hope Father Tomasz backs me.

say: I'd say nobody wants a **machine** playing at their mother's funeral.
I'd tell people to **look after each other** instead of waiting for government.
think: Some churches already use a **self-playing organ** for hymns, and ours could follow.
The **parish council** controls the money, not Father Tomasz.
do: Run the **children's choir** and help with the parish hall.
Refuse to learn any **computer tools** for the job.
S1.quote: Mr Hartmann (the parish treasurer) would buy a self-playing organ tomorrow if it saved the parish four hundred euros a month.
fieldNote: His risk is a **cost-cutting treasurer**, not a smarter machine.
He argues for human playing through **pastoral care** at funerals.
He leans on **community and family**, not government, true to his outlook.

steps.text: Offer to run a children's choir at St Michael's
Keep playing village weddings with Josef's folk band
Ask Father Tomasz to back the live organist at council

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we must hold onto our families and our church, because the companies won't look after us. I'd say it to the choir and to Josef's band. I don't trust governments to fix it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, if people lose their jobs in two years, the collection drops, the weddings get smaller and the band gets fewer bookings. A robot doesn't come for the organ until 2031, but the money for the organist goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back, delay buying a car, and keep our three months. I'd talk to Marta about a smaller wedding, in the parish hall, with the band playing for free. I'd look for steady work alongside, maybe at my cousin's joinery, carrying and sanding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for the music itself, but for whether anyone can still pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Marta feel about a smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta would say it's fine, but her mother would be upset. My fiancée Marta has wanted a wedding with two hundred guests since she was eight, and I'd have to ask for sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help if it was offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, for a while. But I'd rather work with my hands at my cousin's joinery than take money for nothing. That's how I was brought up.

say: I'd tell people to hold onto **families and church**, because companies won't.
I'd say I don't trust **governments** to fix it either.
think: Job losses mean the **collection drops** and wedding bookings fall.
Robots come in **2031**, but the money for an organist goes first.
do: **Delay** buying a car and protect three months of savings.
Plan a **smaller wedding** in the parish hall with Marta.
Take **joinery work** at my cousin's workshop alongside the organ.
feel: **Anxious** about whether anyone can still **pay for music**.
S2.quote: My fiancée Marta has wanted a wedding with two hundred guests since she was eight, and I'd have to ask for sixty.
fieldNote: He sees his risk through **parishioners' jobs**, not robot organists.
A **smaller wedding** is a painful concession he'd make.
He prefers **family work** over government help, as his outlook suggests.

steps.text: Delay buying a car and keep three months saved
Plan a sixty-guest wedding in the parish hall with Marta
Work part-time at his cousin's joinery workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and parishes should start planning now, and look after their own. I'd also say people should learn real trades, things you do with your hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time. The church will shrink, but I'll still be needed for funerals and weddings for a good while. Robots come around 2034, and I don't think the parish buys one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep playing and marry Marta next year as planned. I'd ask my cousin about learning joinery properly, a few days a week, as a second trade. I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can live with it. Five years is a long time in a small town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why joinery, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my cousin's busy and hands are hands. An organ pedal and a chisel both need feet and fingers that know what they're doing, and a computer can't learn that from a book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you give up the organ eventually?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never fully. Even if they paid me nothing, I'd play on Sundays. I'd just need the joinery to eat.

say: I'd tell families and parishes to **plan now** and look after their own.
I'd urge people to learn **real trades** with their hands.
think: I'll still be needed for **funerals and weddings** for a good while.
Robots come around **2034**, and the parish won't buy one.
do: Keep **playing** and marry Marta next year as planned.
Learn **joinery** with my cousin a few days a week.
S3.quote: An organ pedal and a chisel both need feet and fingers that know what they're doing, and a computer can't learn that from a book.
fieldNote: Five years lets him treat **joinery** as a second trade, not a rescue.
He'd **play for free** if needed, showing how much the church means.
He doesn't expect the parish to **buy robots** at all.

steps.text: Marry Marta next year as already planned
Learn joinery at his cousin's workshop three days a week
Keep playing for Sunday mass and funerals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for sensible people to prepare, and that's on families, not the state. I'd keep it simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels far away. By then the church is smaller, and maybe I play for two parishes. I'd be thirty-seven with children, hopefully, and a second trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, marry Marta, and see how things look in a few years. I'd learn joinery slowly. I'm not rushing into anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back of my mind. Ten years is a long time to worry about something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not rushing. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both, I'll admit. Ten years is long enough that I'd rather spend the first two of them getting married than worrying about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Music and a trade, both. If my children can play the organ on Sunday and fix a door on Monday, they'll always have work in a town like ours.

I'd say preparing is on **families**, not the state.
think: By then the church is **smaller** and I might play for two parishes.
I'd be **thirty-seven** with children, hopefully, and a second trade.
do: Keep going **as I am** and marry Marta.
**Wait** a few years before any big change.
feel: **Uneasy** at the back of his mind, since ten years is long to worry.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I'd rather spend the first two of them getting married than worrying about computers.
fieldNote: The long timeline makes him **wait and see**, which he half admits is a hope.
He wants his **children** to have both music and a trade.
Marriage comes **before** any career planning for him.

steps.text: Keep playing at St Michael's and with Josef's band
Marry Marta and start a family
Wait two years before deciding on a second trade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because people would lose their jobs before the parish or families had time to adjust, and the collection and the weddings would dry up. What would help is the parish and the families pulling together, and maybe more apprenticeships in trades so people like me have a second skill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For a lot of people in our town, the church is where they'll go when things get hard. Somebody will still need to play the hymns.

headlineQuote: If my children can play the organ on Sunday and fix a door on Monday, they'll always have work in a town like ours.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old part-time church organist** who also plays accordion at village weddings.
He's **engaged to Marta**, has about three months saved and depends on a shrinking parish collection.
He's **traditional** and trusts family and church over government, and never uses AI.
He expects **parishioners' job losses** to hit his income before any robot organist could.
He reaches for **joinery** with his cousin as a second trade and wants his children to learn both.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the collection and wedding bookings would dry up too fast.
whatWouldHelp: **Parish and families** pulling together in hard times.
More **trade apprenticeships** so musicians can learn a second skill.
